lesson.title: Where Does 1.96 Come From? Finding the Critical Value
lesson.summary: A critical value is the boundary z-score on the standard normal curve that cuts off exactly the tail area needed to leave the chosen confidence level in the middle.
lesson.body:
The margin of error formula relies on a critical value, and earlier chapters simply supplied the standard numbers, 1.645, 1.96, and 2.576, without explaining where they come from. This chapter fills that gap. A critical value is the boundary point on a reference distribution, the standard normal curve for the intervals in this unit, that separates the central region matching your confidence level from the tail regions that fall outside it.

Picture the standard normal curve. To be C% confident, the interval needs to be built wide enough to capture the central C% of the area under that curve, symmetric around the mean of zero. That leaves (100 minus C) percent split evenly between the two tails, one on each side. The critical value, called z-star, is exactly the z-score at the boundary of that central region: the value such that the area to its right equals half of the leftover tail probability.

For a 95% confidence level, the leftover tail probability is 1 minus 0.95, which is 0.05, split evenly into two tails of 0.025 each. The critical value z-star needs 0.025 of area to its right, which is the same as saying the cumulative area to its left is 1 minus 0.025, or 0.975. Looking up 0.975 in a standard normal table, finding the z-score whose cumulative probability equals 0.975, gives z-star equals 1.96, exactly the value used throughout this unit. The same logic gives the other two standard values: for 90% confidence, the tails hold 0.05 each, and the z-score with cumulative area 0.95 is 1.645. For 99% confidence, the tails hold 0.005 each, and the z-score with cumulative area 0.995 is 2.576.

Applying z-star equals 1.96 back to the transit survey confirms the earlier work: with standard error approximately 0.0217, the margin of error is 1.96 times 0.0217, which is approximately 0.0425, giving the 95% confidence interval of 0.2075 to 0.2925 computed in earlier chapters. The critical value is the piece of the calculation that makes the margin of error actually correspond to the confidence level being claimed. Using the wrong critical value, say, using 1.645 while claiming 95% confidence, would produce an interval that does not actually capture the true parameter 95% of the time in the long run, even though the arithmetic would look fine on the surface.
